title: What pattern hides in a square of four calendar numbers?
description: A square of four numbers is taken from a calendar, and the numbers along its two diagonals are multiplied. The board tries another square, writes the numbers with letters, and multiplies out both diagonals to see why the pattern holds.
teaching_notes: One idea: label the four numbers with one letter, multiply out both diagonals, and compare. Watch for students who stop after a few examples and call the pattern proved.

source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 4)
video_script.why: The child can multiply out two brackets, but has not yet used letters to explain a pattern seen in a calendar.
video_script.substitution: Label the four numbers with one letter, as the book's hint says, and multiply out each diagonal by multiplying every term by every term.
video_script.anchor: the calendar square of four numbers from the book, with its two diagonals
video_script.payoff_line: The two diagonal multiplications are always seven apart.

final_answer.value: The diagonal products always differ by 7, because (a + 1)(a + 7) − a(a + 8) = 7
final_answer.spoken: the two diagonal multiplications are always seven apart

maths_rules: square labelled a, a + 1 over a + 7, a + 8
video_script.design: One idea: label the square with one letter and multiply out both diagonals. The calendar square stays on the board through the idea part. The final comparison is left until the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a calendar.
<bookmark mark='square'/>Look at the square of four numbers: four, five, eleven and twelve.
<bookmark mark='dia'/>Along one diagonal, four times twelve is forty eight. Along the other, five times eleven is fifty five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will other squares of four numbers show a pattern too?

beats.colours: the +1 arrow and the +7 arrow in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='arrows'/>In a calendar, the next day is one more. The same day next week is seven more.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>Call the top left number eigh. The square holds eigh, eigh plus one, eigh plus seven, and eigh plus eight.

beats.on_screen: Given: any square of four numbers in a calendar
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, any square of four numbers in a calendar.

beats.on_screen: To find: what the diagonal multiplications show, and why

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find what the diagonal multiplications show, and why.

marks.square: a new square is drawn around 3, 4, 10 and 11

narration: <bookmark mark='square'/>Step one, try another square. Take three, four, ten and eleven.
<bookmark mark='dia'/>Three times eleven is thirty three, and four times ten is forty.

beats.colours: the two diagonals in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step two, write the diagonals with letters. One diagonal is eigh times eigh plus eight.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The other is eigh plus one, times eigh plus seven.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Step three, multiply out the first. Eigh times eigh plus eight is eigh squared plus eight eigh.

marks.parts: a², 7a, a and 7 appear as the four parts
marks.last: a and 7 are written for the one in the first bracket

beats.colours: the like terms in one colour
narration: <bookmark mark='parts'/>Step four, multiply out the second. Eigh times eigh is eigh squared, and eigh times seven is seven eigh.
<bookmark mark='last'/>One times eigh is eigh, and one times seven is seven.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Seven eigh plus eigh is eight eigh, so we get eigh squared plus eight eigh plus seven.

marks.pick: a = 4 is chosen, and 4 × 12 = 48 and 5 × 11 = 55 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='pick'/>Step five, put the first square back in the question. Take eigh as four. Four times twelve is forty eight, and five times eleven is fifty five.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>Eigh squared plus eight eigh plus seven is sixteen plus thirty two plus seven, which is fifty five.

beats.on_screen: Answer: the diagonal products are always seven apart, because (a + 1)(a + 7) - a(a + 8) = 7
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The two diagonal multiplications are always seven apart.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Eigh plus one times eigh plus seven, minus eigh times eigh plus eight, is seven.
